parole.significato: The rain lily (Zephyranthes atamasco).
parole.testo: From Powhatan (+ the English word lily).

parole.significato: A mixture of (frequently rancid) fish parts and blood, dumped into the water as groundbait to attract predator fish, su…
parole.testo: Originally American English, from the 1850s. Perhaps from Powhatan.

parole.significato: A sachem or leader in certain Native American groups.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Powhatan [Term?].

parole.significato: Any of various deciduous hardwood trees of the genera Carya and Annamocarya, one species of which, Carya illinoinensis,…
parole.testo: A shortening of pockerchicory/pokickery/pohickery, from Powhatan pawcohiccora.

parole.significato: A food made from hulled corn (maize) kernels soaked in lye water, rinsed, then cooked and eaten; or, the rinsed kernels…
parole.testo: First recorded in 1629. From Powhatan ("Virginia Algonquian"), though the exact source word is in question: suggestions include uskatahomen, appuminnéonash (“parched corn”), and rokohamin (“parched, ground corn”), the last yielding also the unclipped rockahominy.

parole.significato: The fruit of various American passionflowers, probably Passiflora incarnata and Passiflora lutea.
parole.testo: Perhaps borrowed from Powhatan.

parole.significato: moccasin (type of shoe)
parole.testo: Clipping of moccasin, from Powhatan makasin.

parole.significato: A type of shoe design where there is a seam running around the top of the shoe.
parole.testo: From moc + toe, from Powhatan makasin; see there for more.

parole.testo: From Powhatan makasin, mockasin, mawhcasuns (plural), from Proto-Algonquian *maxkeseni. The word is cognate with Massachusett mohkisson, mokussin, Mi'kmaq mksɨn, Munsee mahkusin, Ojibwe makizin. First appears c. 1612 in the writings of John Smith. parole.significato: Any American marsupial of the family Didelphidae in the order Didelphimorphia.
parole.testo: From Powhatan aposoum (“white animal”), from Proto-Algonquian *wa·p-aʔθemwa (“white dog”); compare Ojibwe waabasim (“white dog”).

parole.significato: The orange fruit of any of various species of trees in the genus Diospyros, especially Diospyros kaki (the kaki or Japa…
parole.testo: From Powhatan pichamins, pushemins, pasimenan (“dried fruit”), for the first element, compare Proto-Algonquian *paᐧʔsamwa (“dry”). The second element is from the same Proto-Algonquian root *-imin (“fruit, berry”) as Unami ximin.

parole.significato: A Native American woman.
parole.testo: After Pocahontas, whose name is a borrowing from Powhatan Pokachantesu (literally “she is playful”).

parole.significato: The poke, Phytolacca americana (formerly Phytolacca decandra).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Powhatan pocan, poughkone. Doublet of puccoon.

parole.significato: Pokeweed, and its berries.
parole.testo: Clipping of pocan (“pokeweed”) or directly borrowed from Powhatan pocan. See pocan for more.

parole.significato: A poisonous North American plant, Phytolacca americana, with reddish stems, broad leaves, clusters of white flowers, an…
parole.testo: From poke + weed. The first element is from Powhatan pocan.

parole.significato: A baked or fried cornbread (bread made of cornmeal), often made without milk or eggs.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Powhatan apones, appoans (“bread”), from Proto-Algonquian *apwa·n (“thing which has been baked or roasted”), whence also Abenaki abôn (“bread”).

parole.significato: Any one of several plants yielding a red pigment which is used by the North American Indians, such as bloodroot (Sangui…
parole.testo: From Virginia Algonquian i.e. Powhatan poughkone. Related to poke, pocan.

parole.significato: An omnivorous, nocturnal mammal native to the Americas, of the genus Procyon, typically with a mixture of gray, brown,…
parole.testo: From arocoun (1608), from Powhatan ärähkun, from ärähkuněm (“he scratches with his hands”).

parole.significato: White beads of low value made from shells, formerly used for ornaments and currency by Native Americans of colonial Vir…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Powhatan rawrenock (“things rubbed smooth by hand”).

parole.significato: Parched cornmeal.
parole.testo: From Powhatan ("Virginia Algonquian") rokohamin (“parched, ground corn”), listed in William Strachey's vocabulary of Powhatan. Compare hominy.

parole.significato: Any of several small turtles of the families Emydidae and Geoemydidae found throughout the world.
parole.testo: From torup (“snapping turtle native to North America, especially the common snapping turtle (Chelydra serpentina)”) or from its etymon Powhatan *tōrəp (“sea turtle”) + possibly English -ine (suffix forming derivative or diminutive nouns), perhaps influenced by Latin terra (“dry land; soil; planet Ea

parole.significato: The edible root of a plant of species Peltandra virginica, used by Native Americans of colonial-era Virginia.
parole.testo: From Powhatan tockawhoughe. The "person" sense implies that such a person was so poor as to be reduced to eating the root.

parole.significato: A chief of an American Indian tribe in colonial Virginia and Maryland.
parole.testo: Apparently borrowed from Powhatan wirowántĕsu (“he is rich”), from wiro (“to be rich”).

parole.significato: A particular plant formerly grown by Native Americans of Virginia and Maryland, thought to be a variety of squash.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Carolina Algonquian macócqwer (plural) or Powhatan mahcawq (“small pumpkin”), or from a combination of the two.
